source.title: Statistical Mechanics of Deep Linear Neural Networks: The Backpropagating Kernel Renormalization

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study sweeps network width and training-set size and measures generalization error, using an equilibrium Gibbs/statistical-mechanics method rather than the original studies' methods. It reports both monotone width results and double descent near capacity in ReLU simulations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports width, depth, and sample-size sweeps of generalization error, which are recorded below. Epoch-wise generalization curves are not reported; Langevin iterations are used to sample the Gibbs distribution, not as an epoch-wise test. Comparisons with Gaussian-process theory and cited results from other work are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: An equilibrium Gibbs/Langevin analysis with simulations sweeps width (linear and ReLU nets) and training-set size, and reports generalization error. This bears on model-wise double descent (V1) and sample-wise harm near the interpolation threshold (V3). It also gives text-only evidence on noise and regularization (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: Largely right. In deep linear nets the error is monotone in width, with direction set by σ: it can improve with width even while interpolating. A sample-size divergence at α0=1 resembles double descent, but the authors say it is not genuine. Finite temperature regularizes this divergence. ReLU nets pushed near capacity show genuine double descent, which the scalar-renormalization approximation misses and fits only on the right side.
record.recipe_differences: Equilibrium Gibbs/Bayesian weight-space analysis and Langevin sampling, rather than the original studies' training-and-sweep procedure; the paper also proposes an approximate BPKR for ReLU networks.
record.method_sensitivity: The direction of the width trend changes with weight-noise parameter σ in the reported sweeps. Sample-size behavior is task-dependent. ReLU double descent is reported when the network is pushed near its capacity/interpolation region; the approximation's agreement also worsens there.

fits_no_version.finding: Depth sweeps in linear (and ReLU) nets give monotone error: decreasing, increasing to a finite limit, or diverging, depending on σ and α.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In deep linear networks, depth-wise generalization error is monotone, with direction set by the weight-noise regime.

record.problems: Most reported curves are figure-only in the supplied text, with no extractable numerical curve values. Several width sweeps are in settings the paper says have zero training error throughout, while the capacity-proximal ReLU double-descent evidence is simulation-only and the proposed approximation fails there. The paper reports error bars for Fig. 6 but not for the other cited curves.

untested.parts: Epoch-wise curves. Langevin iterations only sample the Gibbs distribution.
Model classes other than neural networks; no capacity sweep across classes.
No single effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
Multiple or triple peaks. Whether optimally tuned regularization removes the peak across the whole α0 axis (only error vs T at a few α0 is shown).
Architectures beyond fully connected linear/ReLU nets with 1–5 layers. Standard SGD training.

missing.what: ReLU width sweep at α0>1 (N0=100, P=200): monotone error with N, decreasing at σ=1 and increasing at σ=1.3, with no peak.
Generalization error vs temperature (regularization) at several α0. Optimal T>0 for α0 near 1 and T=0 for small α0.
Analytic result: the divergence at α0=1 is bias-dominated and driven by teacher label noise σ0, scaling as |1−α0|^-1. The authors say the persistence arises because L2 is scaled by T.
ReLU depth sweeps L=1–15 (approximation fails at large L).

record.verdict_notes: All curves are figure-only. The record's V4 challenge from W1–W2 is removed: those sweeps never cross an interpolation threshold. V1 is not challenged by W1–W6 for the same reason; the absence of a peak there reflects sweep range, not failure.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test all deep-network architectures or training procedures. Its results concern deep linear networks and selected ReLU networks, often with one hidden layer.
Test error over training epochs or training time.
The effect is examined in the paper's specific linear-network tasks and input distributions, not across arbitrary tasks or models.
The study considers deep linear and ReLU networks, not a broad survey of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as a predictor of peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.

The study varies weight-noise/regularization parameters and discusses finite-temperature regularization, but does not test whether label noise or variance drives the double-descent peak, whether peaks split, or whether optimally tuned regularization eliminates the peak.
The study does not show that counting effective parameters turns the second descent into an ordinary U-shaped curve.

relationships.condition: One-hidden-layer ReLU nets with small N0 (=20), P=300, swept across N≈α0 on three tasks
relationships.reason: Simulations show a peak near the interpolation threshold with a fall on both sides (W7–W9). For the linear-teacher task the global minimum is on the left side.
relationships.display_finding: Test error peaked near interpolation and decreased on either side across three tasks; the linear-teacher task achieved its global minimum below the threshold.

relationships.condition: Width sweeps in deep linear nets and in ReLU nets that interpolate at all N
relationships.reason: Linear nets have no width-wise threshold, so the authors say genuine double descent does not occur. Past interpolation, error falls with width only at low σ (W1, W3, W5) and rises at high σ (W2, W4, W6).
relationships.display_finding: Linear networks lacked a width-dependent interpolation threshold, while post-interpolation error decreased with width at low σ and increased at high σ.
